title: Highly fragmented European wetlands with uneven restoration needs.

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Downloaded and opened three GeoPackages from the authors' GitHub source_data folder. eu_design_based_area_estimation_samples.gpkg: 10,975 points (WGS84 coordinates), columns Code_18 (CORINE class), Class (the paper's map prediction), reference (expert label, 8 classes: 7,622 non-wetland, 438 inland marshes, 555 peatbogs, 399 salt marshes, 199 salines, 403 intertidal flats, 723 moors/heathland, 636 inland water). Disturbance file: 10,938 points; column distur gives 2,157 least / 423 intermediate / 134 most disturbed among 2,714 wetland points. Country file: 10,938 points, CNTR_ID with 38 countries (ES 1,342 down to LU 6). Map-vs-reference crosstab gives 94.1% unweighted agreement. ERDA file listing via its JSON endpoint: a single 55.7 GB EUwet_dist_merged.gpkg plus two style files. GitHub repo has no licence; DataCite record has no rights field.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: That the reference labels were made by on-screen expert interpretation of high-resolution Google imagery following CORINE nomenclature; that distur is the interpreted disturbance reference rather than the mapped value (inferred from the column name and the design-based estimator, not confirmed); the 101,000 CORINE-labelled training points and their Sentinel feature stacks, which are not released; 96.6% area-weighted overall accuracy. Not checked: the internal tile size of the AlphaEarth embedding files, so the network cost of feature extraction is an estimate.

a1_downloadable.note: Checked: the three labelled-point GeoPackages (1.2–1.3 MB each) download from GitHub with no login. The 55.7 GB map on ERDA (University of Copenhagen archive) is public but over the size cap; it isn't needed.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: Checked: the 'reference' column (wetland type, 8 classes) and the 'distur' column (3 disturbance levels) are already present per point. Nothing has to be built.

a3_inputs_present.note: Partial pass. The files hold only coordinates, no satellite features. Features have to be pulled from a public raster, such as the AlphaEarth 64-dimensional 2018 embeddings (open COG (cloud-optimised GeoTIFF) files on Source Cooperative, no login). That's about 11k automated windowed reads, not identifier lookups, but it is real work and the network cost is unverified.

a4_units_stated.note: Categorical labels, so no units to get wrong. Class codes follow CORINE Land Cover nomenclature; the code-to-name map is in the 'Class Label' column (checked).

a5_enough_rows.note: Checked: 10,975 labelled points for classification, of which 3,353 are wetland. The smallest class (salines) has 199. Disturbance has 2,714 wetland points, with only 134 in the 'most disturbed' level.

a6_fits_laptop.note: The table is tiny. The only heavy step is reading embeddings from cloud COGs, which may move tens of GB over the network (not stored). A tree model or logistic regression runs on CPU in seconds.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: Area sample: 10,975 matches the paper's N_val = 10,975 exactly. The disturbance and country files have 10,938 (37 fewer), which is unexplained but small. Unweighted agreement of 94.1% matches the ERDA description's 94%.

a8_label_provenance.note: Per the paper, labels were assigned by expert visual interpretation, independent of model training. The paper's model was trained on separate CORINE points. Caveat: Code_18 (the CORINE map class) is a map product that sampling was stratified on, and 'Class' is the paper's model output; both must be excluded as features.

B1.why: Three small GeoPackages joining on fid. Features must come from a separate embedding raster; there is no feature table.

B2.why: GeoPackages opened first try with sqlite3; WGS84 points, clean integer codes (checked).

B3.why: One expert interpreter, one protocol, CORINE nomenclature; ambiguous cases jointly reviewed (paper text).

B4.why: No censored values; categorical labels. Disturbance is -1 only for water and non-wetland, by design (checked).

B5.why: One point per row and no repeated coordinates expected from stratified random sampling. Not explicitly deduplicated.

B6.why: README documents required columns. The meaning of distur (reference vs mapped) is not stated explicitly.

C1.why: A cross-country transfer test is informative either way, but the headline accuracy comparison against the map is marginal.

C2.why: Wetland mapping from satellite is a busy remote-sensing field. The paper's own map is open, but its trained model and features aren't released.

C3.why: Weak angle: disturbance-level prediction and country transfer on expert points. Likely novel for these points, but not for the task.

C4.why: Labels need expert on-screen interpretation of each point; CORINE updates every six years at 25-hectare minimum units.

C5.why: The paper's map prediction ('Class' column) is a baseline at every point: 94.1% unweighted agreement (computed).

D1.why: AlphaEarth Foundations satellite embeddings, open COGs 2017–2025 on Source Cooperative (search result, not opened).

D2.why: Embeddings are precomputed per 10-m pixel; sample once, then fit a head on CPU.

D3.why: Embeddings are CC-BY 4.0, but the labelled points carry no licence (GitHub repo and ERDA record checked).

E1.why: Leave-country-out or leave-region-out split from the CNTR_ID column (seen, 38 countries).

E2.why: 16 countries have over 150 points each (checked counts).

E3.why: Majority class (69% non-wetland) and the paper's map prediction at each point.

E4.why: Single interpreter per point; no replicate labels released, so interpreter disagreement can't be estimated.

E5.why: Intertidal flats and salines should be near-trivial (map agreement 97% and 92%); peatbog vs moor confusion is known.

E6.why: Label shuffle and embedding-noise replacement are easy on an 11k-row table.

E7.why: LUCAS 2018 in-situ land-cover survey points include wetland classes; independent field visits (cited in paper).

E8.why: The map-vs-reference confusion matrix reproduces 94.1% unweighted; the repo scripts reproduce the 96.6% weighted figure.

G1.why: Geographic coordinates (WGS84) and ISO-style country codes; no biological identifiers.

G2.why: LUCAS 2018 topsoil carbon and land-cover points, joinable on coordinates; the paper used ~22,000 soil-carbon measurements.

G3.why: Point-to-pixel join is clean; point-to-LUCAS needs nearest-neighbour matching within a distance threshold.

G4.why: Could ask whether embedding-predicted disturbance tracks measured topsoil carbon loss; plausible but loosely joined.

H1.why: 7,622 non-wetland and 2,157 undisturbed points recorded alongside positives (checked).

H2.why: 38 countries, from Iceland to Turkey; one interpretation team, though.

H3.why: Claim is precise: wetland type and disturbance as judged by one expert from 2018-era imagery.

H4.why: Paper documents the sampling design; interpreter subjectivity and the 25-hectare CORINE frame are only partly discussed.

I1.why: EU Nature Restoration Law national planners and the Global Wetland Center (Copenhagen); none have stated a need for a point model.

I2.why: A better disturbance classifier could refine restoration candidate areas; the map already exists.

I3.why: Per-class F1 roughly matches mapping decisions; area estimation needs design-based weighting, not plain accuracy.

I4.why: The paper's gradient-boosting model already reaches 94%; extra gains from embeddings may be small.

J1.why: Geospatial feature extraction, then tabular modelling; grouped splits are real but the backbone is fixed.

J2.why: Remote sensing of wetlands is outside the molecular-biology focus; would need a domain checker.

J3.why: An embedding table at 11k expert points is shareable even if the model doesn't beat the map.

J4.why: One to two weeks is plausible; not yet written down.

J5.why: No kill date recorded in NOTES.md yet.

existing_models.name: Kovács et al. XGBoost (gradient-boosted trees) wetland map (this paper)
existing_models.score_and_split: 96.6% area-weighted overall accuracy on 10,975 independent stratified expert points (94.1% unweighted, computed from the file). The model was trained on 101,000 CORINE-labelled points.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: CORINE's 25-hectare minimum mapping unit and labelling bias against small, managed patches; inland marshes have the lowest precision (67% per the ERDA description).

existing_models.name: European Wetland Map (EWM, Tegetmeyer et al. 2025, Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.14745285)
existing_models.score_and_split: Compiled from existing sources rather than a trained model; accuracy not retrieved.

backbone.name: AlphaEarth Foundations Satellite Embedding V1 (64-dim annual 10-m embeddings, 2018 layer)
backbone.hardware: Laptop CPU; network reads from public S3 cloud storage
backbone.licence: Embeddings CC-BY 4.0; labelled points unlicensed (no LICENSE in repo)

integration.partner_dataset: LUCAS 2018 topsoil organic carbon and land-cover survey (EU in-situ points)
integration.join_key: Coordinates (nearest LUCAS point within a set distance)
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Does disturbance predicted from satellite embeddings at expert-checked wetland points track measured topsoil carbon loss across Europe?

controls.positive_control: Intertidal flats and salines should come out near-perfect (map agreement 97% and 92% at these points); a non-wetland vs water split should be trivial.
controls.negative_control: Shuffle labels within country and confirm a collapse to the majority-class baseline; drop Code_18 and Class from the features to rule out leakage.
controls.external_validation: LUCAS 2018 in-situ land-cover points with wetland classes, held out entirely.

honest_claim_h3: Predicts the wetland type and disturbance level that one expert team would assign from 2018 high-resolution imagery at stratified random points in 38 European countries, not field-verified wetland condition.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use precomputed satellite image summaries at expert-checked points to predict wetland type and how disturbed it is, and test transfer across countries.
plain_idea.train_on: For each of 10,975 points across 38 European countries (verified), a 64-number summary of the 2018 satellite signal at that 10-metre pixel, taken from a public precomputed embedding layer.
plain_idea.predict: One of 8 land classes (6 wetland types, water or non-wetland) and, for 2,714 wetland points, a 3-level human-disturbance score. Both were assigned by an expert looking at high-resolution imagery.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: EU restoration planners need wetland condition maps. Learning whether a generic satellite embedding matches a bespoke model, and whether it transfers between countries, tells mappers if they can skip custom feature engineering.

more_or_better_data.why: Our labels are 10,975 expert points, versus the paper's 101,000 noisier CORINE-derived training points. That's fewer rows, but better labels and the only disturbance labels.

confidence_score.why: Single interpreter per point and no replicate labels, so there's no basis for calibrated per-point confidence beyond standard model probabilities.

models_beatable.why: The 2026 gradient-boosting map reaches 94.1% unweighted on these points; the weakest classes are inland marshes (precision 67%) and moors. Gains are possible there, not overall.

guaranteed_improvement.why: The paper's model and feature stacks aren't released, so we can't give our model everything it saw plus more; only its map output is a baseline.

label_elsewhere.sources: LUCAS in-situ land-cover survey (known resource, cited in the paper as d'Andrimont 2020) has wetland land-cover classes at field-visited points; CORINE Land Cover 2018 covers all of Europe but is itself a mapped product.
label_elsewhere.why: LUCAS field points give an independent, ground-visited test set for wetland type, beyond the paper's screen-interpreted sample.

risks: Code_18 (the CORINE class) was used to stratify sampling and strongly predicts the label, so including it as a feature would inflate scores.
The 'Class' column is the paper's model output, and using it as a feature would just distil that map.
Points close together in the same wetland complex share imagery, so random splits leak through spatial autocorrelation.
AlphaEarth embeddings were trained on global data that might include labels correlated with CORINE, so part of the signal could be inherited rather than learned.
leakage_plan.split: Hold out whole countries (CNTR_ID column, seen in the country GeoPackage, 38 values), or group countries into biogeographic regions and hold out regions.
checks: Shuffle labels within country and confirm a collapse to the majority-class baseline.
Compare random-split and leave-country-out scores; a large gap means spatial leakage.
Train on Code_18 alone to measure how much the stratification variable explains.
leakage_plan.verdict: Manageable: the leaky columns are obvious and a country column exists for grouped splits.

success_criteria.metric: Macro-averaged F1 over the 6 wetland classes on leave-country-out splits, because restoration mapping cares about each wetland type, not about the dominant non-wetland class.
success_criteria.baselines: Majority class (69% non-wetland, macro F1 near 0); the paper's map 'Class' at the same points (94.1% unweighted accuracy, per-class F1 computable from the file; ERDA reports a 73–95% F1 range).
success_criteria.success: Macro wetland F1 at least 0.03 above the paper's map on leave-country-out, or disturbance-level macro F1 at least 0.6 with no published baseline.
success_criteria.kill: If embeddings fall more than 0.05 macro F1 below the paper's map after the first leave-country-out run, stop.

ambitious.why: Publishes continental wetland-mapping methods. It would need embeddings to clearly beat bespoke features on held-out countries, plus validation against LUCAS.

realistic.journal: International Journal of Applied Earth Observation and Geoinformation
realistic.why: Takes benchmark studies of foundation-model embeddings for specific land-cover tasks; fits a cross-country transfer result.

fallback.journal: arXiv preprint plus a NeurIPS/ICLR climate-change AI workshop
fallback.why: A negative result that generic embeddings underperform bespoke wetland features is still a workshop-sized finding.

pitch.headline: 10,975 expert-checked points across 38 countries, with wetland type and 3-level human disturbance, sitting in 4 MB of GeoPackages.
pitch.what_makes_the_data_unusual: Independent stratified sample with disturbance labels for 2,714 wetland points (134 most disturbed), plus the paper's map prediction at every point for a free baseline. Labelling method rests on the paper text.
pitch.the_win: Wetland macro F1 at least 0.03 above the paper's map on leave-country-out splits, using only frozen public embeddings.
pitch.even_if_it_fails: We learn whether generic satellite embeddings can replace bespoke wetland features, and which countries the transfer fails in.
pitch.who_wants_it: The Global Wetland Center (Copenhagen) and EU Nature Restoration Law national mapping teams deciding whether to rebuild custom wetland classifiers.

ml_idea: Sample 2018 AlphaEarth 64-dim embeddings at the 10,975 expert reference points. Train a gradient-boosting or logistic head for wetland type and disturbance level with leave-country-out cross-validation, and compare against the paper's map prediction at the same points.

effort.compute_note: Estimated, not timed: embeddings are precomputed, so the cost is about 11k windowed remote reads from COG tiles (tile size unverified, possibly tens of GB transferred). The model runs on an 11k × 64 table.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Read AlphaEarth 2018 embeddings at 100 points, fit a quick model, and check whether peatbog vs moors/heathland separates at all versus the map's own confusion.

verdict_reason: Passes Part A: 10,975 expert labels downloaded and counts match. But this is remote-sensing land cover rather than molecular biology, the labels have no licence, the field is busy, and the likely gain over the paper's 94% map is marginal.
